fields.problem:
Title: Maximum possible number of 1012-element subsets of {1,2,...,2024} such that no three intersect at more than one element

I came across the following problem:

At most how many $1012$-element subsets of $\lbrace 1,2,\dots,2024 \rbrace$ may be chosen such that the intersection of any three subsets has at most one element?

I tried small cases. For example, I considered $3$-element subsets of $\lbrace 1,2,3,4,5,6 \rbrace$. By playing around (see table below), I think I got that for this case, the maximum is 8 subsets:

Essentially, we reach the point that for all triples $(a,b,c)$ at least one of $a-b, b-c, a-c$ are already in two subsets together. However, I have no idea how to prove that this is the maximum amount for even the $\lbrace 1,2,3,4,5,6 \rbrace$ case, and am stumped on how to proceed with the general or $2024$ case.

Intuitively, I feel as though there must be some way to upper-bound the number of subsets and then give a construction that satisfies that upper bound, but I am lost on how to proceed.

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

0019 | Consider a column. Let there be $c_i$ 1's in it. We have $ \sum c_i = kn$ as the sum of the matrix.
0020 | 
0021 | The column contributes ${c_i \choose 3 }$ column-triples, so the total is $ \sum { c_i \choose 3}$.
0022 | 
0023 | By Jensen's inequality, we get $\sum { c_i \choose 3 } \geq 2n { \frac{ \sum c_i } { 2n } \choose 3 } = 2n { \frac{k}{2} \choose 3 }$.
0024 | 
0025 | Consider any 3 rows.
0026 | 
0027 | Since any 3 sets have an intersection of at most 1, these 3 rows can yield at most 1 column triple. Thus, there are at most ${k \choose 3 } $ triples.
0028 | 
0029 | Hence, $ 2n { \frac{k}{2} \choose 3 } \leq \text{ total column triples} \leq { k \choose 3 }$, or that $2n \leq \frac{ 8(k-1) } { (k-4) }$.
0030 | 
0031 | For $k = 5$, the RHS is $\frac{ 8 \times 5}{1} > 2 \times 1012$.
0032 | 
0033 | Thus, we have $k \leq 4$.
0034 | 
0035 | Thus, the maximum for $n \geq 21$ is 4.
0036 | 
0037 | BONUS
0038 | 
0039 | Note that for $n=3$, this argument doesn't work because we always have $6 \leq 8 \frac{ k-1}{k-4}$ for $k > 4$, and so we don't have a bound on $k$. Instead, we approach it in another manner, and count row pairs $(1, 1)$.
0040 | 
0041 | Each row has $n$ 1's, so there are ${n \choose 2}$ pairs. Since there are $k$ rows, so there are $ k { n \choose 2 } $ pairs.
0042 | 
0043 | Consider any 2 columns. Since any 3 sets have an intersection of at most 1, these 2 columns can yield at most 2 pairs of $(1, 1)$. Since there are ${2n \choose 2 }$ pairs of columns, thus there are at most $ 2 { 2n \choose 2 }$ such pairs.
